title.narrative: KEWASNET Förbättrad styrning i kenyanska vattensektorn, fas II
KEWASNET Water Governance Support Programme, phase II

description.narrative:
Kenya Water and Sanitation Civil Society Network (KEWASNET)(Nätverksorganisationen för Kenyas Civilsamhällesorganisationer i Vattensektorn) är det nationella nätverket för ett antal (för närvarande 77) civilsamhällesorganisationer i vattensektorn i Kenya. Sveriges ambassad i Nairobi (härefter EoS) har stött KEWASNET att genomföra ett Program för Förbättrad Styrning i Vattensektorn (Water Governance Support Programme) (härefter WGSP I) under åren 2014 - 2019. EoS emottog ett förslag från KEWASNET för en andra fas av programmet, WGSP II, med en slutlig förhandlad budget om 23 MSEK som gåvostöd i form av program-stöd, innehållande resultat-baserad outsourcing/ vidareförmedling av upp til ca 20% av programbudgeten till medlemsorganisationer, med start i november 2019. En förlängning med budgettillskott av avtalet för WGSP I för att täcka övergångsaktiviteter under juli - oktober 2019 har också genomförts.
WGSP II kommer att fördjupa och kopiera framgångsrika aktiviteter från WGSP I (många av dessa är process-orienterade och tar tid att genomföra), men också identifiera nya öppningar i vattensektorn och ta sig an nya tematiker och geografiska områden. Arbetssättet kommer att vara agilt och adaptivt för att hålla takten med utvecklingen i sektorn..
WGSP II har som mål att verka för hållbar förvaltning av vattenresurser och förbättrad WASH (vattenförsörjning, sanitet och hygien) i Kenya, med fokus på de mest eftersatta i befolkningen. Genom aktiviteter som genomförs av KEWASNETs sekretariat och medlemsorganisationer, med rättighetsbaserade arbetsmetoder, så kommer programmet att från ett civilsamhällesperspektiv stärka WASH- och vattenresursförvaltningsinstitutioner och intressenter, styrningsmekanismer och regelsefterlevnad inom urban sanitet, styrningsmekanismer och modeller för utbyggnad av vatten och sanitet på landsbygden, sektorkoordinering, ansvarsutkrävande, folkets röst, kapacitet hos civilsamhällesorganisationer, och medborgarinflytande i centrala policyprocesser.
Programmet kommer att genomföras på länsnivå, regional nivå, nationell nivå och internationell nivå, med fokus på 10 län främst i centrala och södra/västra Kenya (Kwale, Tharaka-Nithi, Machakos, Makueni, Baringo, Laikipia, Narok, Kakamega, Busia, Nyamira).
Medan WGSP II tematiskt bygger på och skalar upp WGSP I, så föreslår EoS att inte operationellt länka ihop de två avtalen genom konditionalitet för utbetalningar etc. Återbetalning av medel från WGSP I (eventuella rapporterade oanvända medel, utestående förväntade återbetalade WGSP I - medel från Chase Bank-kollapsen 2016 (ca 500 000 SEK) , och möjlig avskrivning av den förlust av ca 500 000 SEK som också gjordes vid Chase Bank--kollapsen, kommer att hanteras separat under en förlängning av WGSP I-avtalet.

The Kenya Water and Sanitation Civil Society Network (KEWASNET) is the national network of (currently 77) water civil society organisations in Kenya. The Embassy of Sweden in Nairobi (EoS hereafter) has supported KEWASNET to implement a Water Governance Support Programme (hereafter WGSP I) during the years 2014 - 2019. EoS received a proposal from KEWASNET for a second phase of the programme, Water Governance Support Programme II, with a final negotiated budget of 23 MSEK as grant programme support over 3 years , including results-based outsourcing/ ongranting of up to around 20% of the budget to member organisations, to start in November 2019. A cost extension of WGSP I covering transition activities in July - October 2019 has also been undertaken.
The Water Governance Support Programme II will deepen and replicate successful activities from WGSP I (many are process-oriented which take time), but also seize new opportunities in the sector and venture into new thematic and geographical areas. The approach will be agile and adaptive to keep up with new developments in the sector.
The WGSP II aims to promote Sustainable Management of Water Resources and Improved WASH (Water, Sanitation and Hygiene) services in Kenya, with a focus on Leaving No-one Behind. Through activities undertaken by its Secretariat and member organisations, using human rights based approaches, the programme will from a CSO perspective strengthen WASH- and WRM institutions and stakeholders, urban sanitation regulatory and compliance environment, rural water and sanitation services provision and regulation, sector coordination, accountability mechanisms, citizens' voice, capacity of CSOs, and public participation in key policy development processes.
The programme will intevene at sub-national/county, regional, national and international levels, with a focus on 10 counties mainly in central and Southern/ Western Kenya (Kwale, Tharaka-Nithi, Machakos, Makueni, Baringo, Laikipia, Narok, Kakamega, Busia, Nyamira).
While the WGSP II thematically builds on and scales out WGSP I, EoS proposes not to link the two agreements operationally through conditions for disbursements etc. Repayment of funds due from WGSP I (any eventual balances, outstanding expected repayments of WGSP I funds from the 2016 Chase Bank collapse amounting to approximately 500 000 SEK, and possible write-off of losses incurred from the same 2016 Chase Bank collapse amounting to approximately 500 000 SEK) will be handled separately under an extension of the WGSP I agreement.

The Water Governance Support Programme II aims to promote Sustainable Management of Water Resources and Improved WASH (Water, Sanitation and Hygiene) services in Kenya. The programme will be anchored on four outcome areas including:
Outcome 1: Improved management of water resources, and water and sanitation services provision Outcome 2: Improved coordination of sector interventions Outcome 3: Improved transparency, integrity, accountability and sector decision making Outcome 4: Strong and active institutions that effectively respond to the SDG ambition.

sector.narrative: Education and training in water supply and sanitation

description.narrative:
KEWASNET was responsible to implement the programme in cooperation with implementing partners: Community Asset Building and Development (CABDA), Centre for Social Planning and Administrative Development (CESPAD), ECO GREEN, Kenya Water and Health Organization (KWAHO), Laikipia Wildlife Forum (LWF), Neighbours Initiative Alliance (NIA) and Wash Alliance Kenya (WAK) whom have been responsible for activities at county level targeting local communities and stakeholders. Despite challenges faced due to the Covid19 pandemic during the core implementation period of the programme, the majority of the planned activities were implemented and have generated positive results. Results are exemplified under each of the planned outcomes of the programme below.
Outcome 1: Improved management of Water Resources, and Water and Sanitation Services provision
1. There is improved governance, management, and leadership in water utility systems. This is attributable to increased understanding of roles and responsibilities of institutions and key water stakeholders and inter county and inter basin learning between stakeholders as an innovation to bring in new knowledge and experiences from other counties on Integrated Water Resource Management (IWRM). 2. In year one, through various capacity building and trainings sessions targeting Water Resources User Associations (WRUAs), Community Forests Associations (CFAs), civil society organisations (CSOs) and champions on integration of water resources, there was increased number of functional and strengthened institutions and stakeholders. Some of the water utilities like Muthambi 4k in Tharaka Nithi County, have managed to curb the loss of nonrevenue water and were ranked as the best performers by the Water Services Regulatory Authority (WASREB) in managing non revenue water. They have also managed to increase their financial base and create a reserve fund, which has boosted improved provision of services through more water connections and improved water system maintenance. 3. In year two, a learning trip was conducted by LWF for twelve community water projects drawn from seven WRUAs to Mutitu Water and Sanitation Company. Mutitu Water and Sanitation Company is a model rural water service provider having transformed from a typical community water project to a regulated water service provider. From the learning exchange, community water projects started adopting household metering to enhance equitable water sharing even in drought seasons. Kiranga water project for instance secured water meters and installed them for domestic water users. 4. Elsewhere, there is improved compliance within the small water utilities on WASREB guidelines through sensitization of various county governments/utilities on WASREB guidelines for water provision in rural and underserved areas. For instance, the three small water utilities trained in Nyamira have started complying with the WASREB guidelines by choosing an appropriate management model. Two groups in Nyamira have started the process of registering as a Water User Association (WUA). This will provide an official status with legal recognition that allows for greater transparency and more effective water sources and resources management. 5. Through the trainings that CESPAD conducted at Enkare Narok WRUA, there is increased change in behaviour, where particularly over 2000 women who were charcoal burners have committed to being environmental conservationists from charcoal users to water and environment champions. CESPAD is continued to build the women's capacity to work on alternative sources of livelihood such as making beads, crocheting, and getting involved in conservation work through tree planting and sensitizing the community. Women groups in Narok were also linked to other development partners for funding of the water resources management (WRM) activities. 6. As a result of the WRUA trainings that were conducted in 2020, new counties expressed interest to be supported with similar trainings. KEWASNET aligned such requests in line with other programmes to enhance sustainability for the established structures.
Outcome 2: Improved coordination of sector interventions
1. CESPAD held three WASH summit engagement forums with Makueni, Machakos and Baringo counties and established a WASH/WRM summit in Baringo with guiding TOR that was adopted by the county government. The forums brought together at least 30 stakeholders each both from the state and non state actors to share on the interventions they have and identify areas of synergies to avoid duplication. As a result, KEWASNET and CESPAD in collaboration with the Baringo CSOs network and the County Government of Baringo increased the awareness, capacity and agency of water consumers (especially women), service providers and other stakeholders to take effective part in constructive governance dialogue on WASH and WRM policy decisions/ budget formulation, project identification and implementation through a countywide cascaded Multi-Stakeholder Platforms. 2. The programme supported one meeting targeting County Executive Committee Members (CECMs) from the County Governments. Through this session different stakeholders from the water sector highlighted priorities in the sector and a unified approach of implementation for various guidelines including Rural Water Supply Guidelines were agreed upon and road map developed. 3. In early 2020, through their implementing partnership with NIA, KEWASNET conducted a Training of Trainers (ToTs) for 20 Health/WASH clubs in 10 schools in Kakamega and Busia Counties. The trained ToTs in turn established the clubs at the school level. The existence of the clubs over a period of three years has seen improved sanitation and hygiene at the school environment through improved hand washing, waste collection and management and clean school environment. 4. As part of learning and contribution to knowledge and information for decision making in the sector, KEWASNET had earlier conducted under this outcome a study on Mapping the nexus between WASH/WRM programming and education, health and environment sectors in Kenya. The study sought to map out the nexus and make practical recommendations on how the various players can work together to strengthen and have functional WRM institutions. The study findings were disseminated throughout the second and third year among other programmes studies as outlined in outcome one. 5. Throughout the period 2020 up until 2022, KEWASNET was a member of and took in the WASH Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) Coordination meetings that supported at a national scale all the WASH IPC related interventions for Covid-19. The forum has since been converted into a WASH coordination forum which KEWASNET is part of and meets regularly to deliberate on WASH issues from across the nation. Overall, KEWASNET found significant value and was able to contribute into improved sector coordination at both the national and sub-national levels through the programme. In a number of instances, this coordination value addition also informed our contributions to pan-african coordination through the Africa Civil Society Network on Water and Sanitation (ANEW), and globally through a variety of platforms including End Water Poverty, Sanitation and Water for All and Fair Water footprints partnership.
Outcome 3: Improved transparency, integrity, accountability and sector decision making in WASH and WRM
1. To fulfill its theory of change, the programme had a component that worked with the duty bearers, rights holders, CSOs and citizens on issues around accountability, integrity, transparency and information for sectors decision making. During the implementation period, KEWASNET in collaboration with KWAHO conducted a number capacity strengthening workshops on Social Accountability in Busia, Kakamega, Tharaka Nithi, Makueni, and Machakos Counties. Some of the immediate results which have been documented include: - organized and capable community groups has been established, with the ability to hold governments to account, efficiently, effectively and coherently using data for evidence in realizing this aspiration. - county and national governments are more responsive in allocation of resources and creating opportunities for constructive citizen engagement in decision making processes including public participation processes. - citizens are able to access and effectively use adequate, reliable and essential information, a major prerequisite for monitoring performance citizens are able to keep track of and evaluate the impacts of government projects, including efficacy, quality and responsiveness of service delivery. 2. As a result of the work around accountability in WASH, KEWASNET and its members developed a book on Social Accountability: A handbook for practitioners in the WASH and Water Resource Management (WRM) sector. The handbook was developed for practitioners in the Water and Sanitation sector to not only guide conversations towards improved service delivery and resource management but also for accelerated elevation of citizen voices through the application of the social accountability tools. Since its formulation and adoption in 2020/21, the book has been utilised by practitioners in the sector and applied yo various groups including the youth parliaments, CSOs among others. It has also been utilized by other programmes and projects within and beyond KEWASNET. 3. KEWASNET conducted two regional media training forums in Coast and Western/Nyanza. The events brought together media professionals from the regions. Apart from setting out the importance of Media in WASH it provided a platform for debate and created an opportunity for peer learning and sharing of best practices in media on WRM and WASH services. The media fraternity made commitments to highlight WASH/WRM issues and ensure that communities get relevant information that surrounds Water rights which has been evident in the recent past. 4. KEWASNET in partnership with NIA, KWAHO, CESPAD, ECOGREEN and WAK coordinated the commemoration other key international days including the Global Handwashing Day, the World Toilet Day, the Menstrual Hygiene Management Day. During the MHM Day at St. Daniel Comboni Primary School in Korogocho informal settlements, in Nairobi county, for instance, the county made a commitment that the government will continue to earmark and increase resources allocated for MHM especially in primary and secondary school going girls. 5. Through the programme period, KEWASNET was able to position itself as an effective advocate for accountability and transparency, especially from the duty bearer perspective. Standout cases includes a petition that was successfully lodged with the National Assembly and Senate committees of Water, challenging the integrity of published Water Resources Regulations 2021. This resulted to the Senate declaring the regulations illegal, and a subsequent public interest litigation by KEWASNET on the same in 2023.
Outcome 4: Strong and active institutions that effectively respond to the SDG ambition
1. To strengthen institutional capacities, during phase I of the programme, KEWASNET had developed the Integrity, Quality and Compliance (IQC) Toolbox that has been applied to its membership since 2015. In 2016 however, a new Water Act 2016 was formulated establishing major changes in the sector. In order to align to the new law, KEWASNET reviewed the IQC Toolbox for future trainings and support to its membership. 2. KEWASNET conducted various study cycles targeting Kwale, Kakamega, Nyamira, Laikipia and Baringo counties reaching out to various stakeholders in the five counties. The overall aim of the study cycles was to induct sector actors on key orientations around SDG 6 and define key priorities for building momentum. The key priority activities identified as part of the County action plan in the target counties include a. Capacity building b. Advocacy c. Data and information management. The study cycle workshops enabled the participants to acquire knowledge on the place of SDG 6 within the broader context of global goals where key priorities for building momentum were identified. The workshops also led to the identification of valuable insights of future needs and gaps to fill in each of the topics. 3. To strengthen Policy and Legislative Environment, CESPAD in collaboration with other implementing partners supported the popularization of the county public policy development guide targeting County Government of Kiambu, Kajiado, Nakuru, Narok and CSOs working on policies in Kenya. The policy formulation guidelines had been developed in phase I of the programme in collaboration with GIZ following the extensive work supporting counties policy formulation initiatives. The platform also offered opportunity to share lessons learnt, case studies and forge a way forward in the development of County public policies especially for those counties that are yet to develop their respective policies. 4. In Laikipia for instance, the County Water Services Bill had stalled for one year following objections by local stakeholders on several provisions contained in the bill. LWF sought to engage its membership drawn from community water projects and other relevant stakeholders to identify any gaps with the current bill and generate a memorandum to the County Executive and Assembly with recommendations to inform any further amendments. Following a series of engagements with the county executives, the water bill was revised with proper inputs from the communities and was adopted by the Laikipia Assembly into the Water Act. NIA on the other hand supported Nanyuki Water and Sanitation Company (NAWASCO) to conduct a customer satisfaction/corruption perception survey develop pro-poor water supply policy review customer service charter and review customer complaints and feedback mechanism. These documents were eventually finalised and adopted by NAWACSO board for operationalisation. 5. One of the greatest achievements under this outcome during the implementation period was the ability to successfully conduct Technical Working Groups (TWGs) and study cycles which not only brought key stakeholders together but also worked to attain necessary solutions to some of the far reaching challenges in the WASH/WRM sector. In 2020 for instance, KEWASNET conducted a TWG on WASH with a focus on Covid-19 outbreak, themed: State of the Nation: WASH and WRM in Kenya under the Microscope. A number of recommendations from the TWG were picked up by key institutions such as WSTF and water service providers (WSPs for implementation partly leading to increased focus on water supply. 6. The programme also supported the upgrading of KEWASNET online M&E system which is currently supporting in the reporting and data management for the organization.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
